title: A critical eye can be worth more than knowing how to use tools
description: Tools produce, designers decide. Why a critical eye is worth more than mastering any tool, and how to practice it.

related.title: Clint Scale
related.body: In practice: an explorable design system, with tokens, components, contrast and governance.

blocks.text: Anyone who works in design is already used to learning new tools.
But there's one skill that stays necessary no matter the tool:
knowing how to evaluate a solution.
Tools produce. Designers decide.
The difference seems simple, but it matters.

blocks.caption: Generating got cheap. The value is in the questions that decide what moves forward.

items: A tool can generate an interface

blocks.text: But someone has to look at it and ask:
Does this make sense?
That's where the critical eye comes in.
The problem with confusing tool mastery with design mastery
You can be great at Figma and still create a bad experience.
You can also be great at an AI tool and generate solutions that don't solve the problem.
Knowing a tool means knowing how to operate that tool.
Knowing design means knowing why you make a given choice.
That difference is even clearer now that so many production tasks can be automated.
What does a designer need to see?

data.lead: Even so, we can ask a few questions.
questions: Does the user know what to do?
Is the most important information clear?
Does the flow demand too many decisions?
Does the system explain what's happening?
Does the content use the language people actually use?
Is there any barrier for people with different needs?
Is the product solving the right problem?
data.outro: These questions don't show up on their own just because an interface looks visually correct.

blocks.text: Critiquing isn't hunting for flaws
There's a difference between critique and opinion.

blocks.caption: Good critique is made of questions, not opinions.

data.analysis: “This information is competing visually with the main action and may make the decision harder.”

blocks.text: Good critique needs criteria.
It can be based on:
A designer doesn't need to like it or dislike it.
They need to be able to explain it.
Good design needs arguments
This also changes how we present our work.
Instead of:
“I chose this solution because I thought it looked cleaner.”
We can say:
“We chose this structure because testing showed people struggled to find the main action. The new hierarchy reduces the number of elements competing for attention.”
Now there's reasoning behind it.
That's especially important when we use AI.
If the tool generated three solutions, we need to explain why we picked one of them.
Data helps sharpen the critical eye
A critical eye doesn't have to be only visual.
We can combine different kinds of evidence.
Data: shows behavior at scale.
Research: shows needs and perceptions.
The more sources of information we have, the better we can evaluate a solution.
Growth is part of this conversation too
Imagine a change increased conversion.
Does that mean the design got better?
Maybe.
But we need to look at the context.
Did retention improve?
Did activation improve?
Did satisfaction change?
Did behavior after conversion change?
A positive metric doesn't end the analysis.
It raises another question.
This kind of thinking is very important in Growth.
Making the number go up isn't enough.
We need to understand what's happening to the experience.
A critical eye prevents “design for design's sake”

items: An interface can follow a trend
It can follow a new visual pattern

blocks.text: But the question is still:
Does this help someone get something done?
If it doesn't, maybe it's just decoration.
Design doesn't need to be complicated to show knowledge.
Often, the best solution is the one that makes the problem simpler for the person using it.
What if AI produces something better than you?
That question can be uncomfortable.
But I think it's important to ask.
Maybe an AI can generate an interface that looks better than what I'd create on my own.
And that's fine.
A designer's job doesn't have to be competing with the machine at producing pixels.
We can use that capability in our favor.
The question becomes:
Can I evaluate this solution better?
Can I spot where it fails?
Can I adapt it to the product's context?
Can I test it with users?
Can I connect this solution to the business goal?
That's a space where experience and judgment still matter.
Design can become more strategic
If production keeps getting faster, we can spend more time on:

items: This doesn't shrink the designer's role

blocks.text: The designer stops being just someone who turns requirements into screens.
They become someone who helps the team decide which experience should exist.
Maybe “good taste” isn't enough
There's an interesting discussion about taste in the age of AI.
I believe taste helps.
But on its own it isn't enough.
A solution can be visually excellent and still not work.

data.after: That's what lets you evaluate a solution more completely.

blocks.text: The tool changes. The problem stays.
A few years from now, we may be using tools that don't even exist today.
Maybe the creative process will be completely different.
But we'll still have people trying to get tasks done.
We'll still have products that need to create value.
That's why I believe learning tools is important.
But learning to think about what we're creating is even more important.
